rationale: Joshua describes Manasseh's daughters inheriting among their brothers in the preceding Zelophehad case; Numbers expressly grants Zelophehad's daughters their father's allotment among his brothers, while Joshua additionally distinguishes remaining Gilead.

relationship: Same-chapter Manasseh boundary introduction and Ephraim holding distinction
rationale: Manasseh's boundary description through Delanath, Jamin, Jassib and Thaphthoth is followed by the particular distinction of an Ephraim holding on Manasseh's border; Thaphthoth and Thapheth are not independently equated.

relationship: Ephraim ownership alongside Manasseh in related allotment notices
rationale: Thapheth on Manasseh's border expressly belongs to Ephraim; the earlier summary describes Ephraim cities amid Manasseh, supplying related cross-tribal ownership language without claiming this border town is a fully surrounded enclave.

relationship: Ephraim possession amid a Manasseh city
rationale: The boundary description expressly places an Ephraim terebinth amid a Manasseh city; the earlier summary describes Ephraim cities within Manasseh, preserving this unit's different tree and town wording.

relationship: Same-chapter northern Manasseh side and shared sea endpoint
rationale: The distinction between southwestern Ephraim and northern Manasseh resumes the preceding Manasseh boundary on the north toward the torrent and sea, now adding Asher and Issachar contacts.

relationship: Manasseh's named towns and later non-possession account
rationale: Both Manasseh accounts include Dor and its dependent settlements and similarly rendered Beth-shean or Beth-shan and Megiddo or Magedon; the latter forms remain distinct and no full town-list equivalence is claimed.

relationship: Manasseh's unremoved Canaanites in town-possession notices
rationale: Both say Manasseh did not possess or destroy the specified towns and that Canaanites began to dwell in the land, retaining each passage's actual named-town list.

relationship: Growing strength followed by subjection without complete removal
rationale: Both state that Israel became strong and subjected the Canaanites while not utterly destroying or completely removing them, preserving the distinct supplied descriptions of that subjection.

relationship: Same-chapter one-lot complaint and Joshua's explicit answer
rationale: The numerous Joseph descendants complain of one lot; Joshua answers that their numbers and strength warrant more, specifying woodland clearing and overcoming the Canaanites' cavalry.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated woodland-clearing answer
rationale: Joshua first directs the numerous people to clear woodland when Ephraim's mountain is cramped; his concluding answer again assigns the woodland for clearing and adds the assurance about overcoming cavalry.

relationship: Same-chapter cavalry objection and stated counter-assurance
rationale: The people object to insufficient mountain space and Canaanite choice cavalry and iron; Joshua's answer expressly acknowledges choice cavalry and declares them stronger, without substituting an unprovided chariot phrase.

relationship: Same-chapter numerous-people claim answered with more than one lot
rationale: Joshua repeats the people's description as numerous and declares they will not have one lot only, directly answering their complaint about a single measured inheritance.

relationship: Same-chapter woodland and cavalry reply to the defined dispute
rationale: The concluding command joins the earlier woodland-clearing proposal with an answer to the people's cavalry objection, preserving both concrete parts of the land-and-strength dialogue.

relationship: Shiloh as the location of Israel's central sanctuary objects
rationale: Joshua describes the congregation pitching the Tent of Testimony at Shiloh; Samuel later describes taking the Lord's ark from Shiloh, without treating the later battle action as the same occasion.

relationship: Same-chapter seven unallotted tribes and seven proposed portions
rationale: The notice of seven tribes without inheritance is answered by the explicit division into seven portions and bringing out a lot before the Lord, without supplying an unstated total of surveyors.

relationship: Same-chapter delay rebuke followed by the practical allocation plan
rationale: Joshua's question about delaying possession leads into appointing surveyors, describing the land and dividing seven portions for lot assignment, identifying the particular response to the rebuke.

relationship: Same-chapter survey command and narrated written report
rationale: Joshua calls for three men from each tribe to travel and describe the land; the later units narrate the surveyors going, recording its cities in seven portions and bringing the scroll back.

relationship: Same-chapter Judah-Joseph sides and Benjamin's intervening lot
rationale: The plan leaves Judah on the southwest and Joseph's sons on the north; Benjamin's first lot is then expressly described as between Judah and Joseph, preserving the given regional arrangement.

relationship: Tribal division by lots commanded and implemented
rationale: Joshua orders seven described portions brought for lot assignment before the Lord; Numbers had commanded division of the land by ancestral-tribe lots between larger and smaller groups.

relationship: Levitical exclusion grounded in assigned divine service
rationale: Joshua says Levi has no territorial portion because the Lord's priesthood is their portion; Numbers addresses the Lord-as-inheritance assurance to Aaron and the tithe-for-service allotment to Levites, retaining those distinct scopes.

relationship: The eastern tribes' already received inheritance
rationale: Both explicitly name Gad, Reuben and half Manasseh as recipients of Moses' eastern grant; Joshua distinguishes them from the seven unallotted tribes and Levites in the current distribution.

relationship: Same-chapter commanded survey and returned city-by-city scroll
rationale: Joshua directs the men to survey and return to him at Shiloh; the narrative then records their survey, city-based seven-part description and delivery of the scroll to Joshua.

relationship: Same-chapter completed description and earlier survey commission
rationale: The surveyors' written city-by-city division fulfills Joshua's instruction to travel and describe the land for distribution, with the later unit specifying seven portions in a scroll.

relationship: Same-chapter casting the lots and the prior announcement
rationale: Joshua casts lots before the Lord at Shiloh, carrying out his announced plan to receive the seven portions and bring out a lot before the Lord.

relationship: Same-chapter Benjamin between the two named established portions
rationale: Benjamin's lot expressly lies between Judah and Joseph's sons, corresponding to the plan that Judah mark the southwest boundary and Joseph the north before the remaining lots are drawn.

relationship: Jordan-Jericho beginning in adjacent tribal boundaries
rationale: Benjamin's northern border begins at Jordan by Jericho, the same explicitly named starting features as Joseph's broader border; their later wilderness and Bethel-luza or Bethon stages are not independently equated.

relationship: Bethel-Luza and Lower Beth-horon within related inheritance routes
rationale: Both route descriptions name Bethel with a Luza form and Lower Beth-horon; Benjamin's Maatarothorech and Joseph's Chatarothite or Aptalim stages remain separate rather than being silently harmonized.

relationship: Explicit Kiriath-baal-Jearim identification on Judah's side
rationale: Benjamin's boundary expressly identifies Kiriath-baal as Kiriath-jearim, a Judah city; the Judah catalog likewise associates Kiriath-baal with Jearim and adds Sotheba, preserving each description.

relationship: Naphtho water spring in the two boundary accounts
rationale: Both name the water spring of Naphtho in their boundary routes; Benjamin's edge of Kiriath-baal and Gasin remain distinct from Judah's mountain-to-Ephron and Baal sequence.

relationship: Spring of Rogel at named boundary stages
rationale: Both boundary descriptions reach the Spring of Rogel; Benjamin's Onnam, Emekraphain, Gaienna and Jebusite-ridge stages are preserved separately from Judah's Achor, Gilgal and Addamin approach.

relationship: Stone of Baion with Reuben qualification in both routes
rationale: Both explicitly name Baion's stone associated with Reuben; Joshua18's sons wording and Bethsamys or Galiloth stages remain distinct from Joshua15's son wording and Beth-hoglah or Beth-arabah stages.

relationship: Northern side of Beth-arabah in both tribal boundaries
rationale: Both boundary descriptions explicitly pass the north side of Beth-arabah; the Benjamin unit continues downward, while Judah's unit also names Beth-hoglah and ascent to Baion's stone.

relationship: Salt Sea-Jordan junction on opposite tribal boundary sides
rationale: Benjamin's southern end reaches the northern Salt Sea ridge at Jordan's edge; Judah's northern boundary begins at the sea ridge and Jordan edge, preserving the distinct side labels and Beth-hoglah detail.

relationship: Same-chapter Benjamin lot opening and complete boundary conclusion
rationale: The Jordan-on-east conclusion identifies the whole inheritance as Benjamin's by divisions, returning to the opening lot attribution between Judah and Joseph before the city catalog begins.

relationship: Jericho in Benjamin's city lot and earlier conquest notice
rationale: Benjamin's catalog names Jericho among its cities; the earlier account describes the city's burning and Rahab's preservation because she hid the spies sent to Jericho, without identifying Betheglio or Amekasis there.

relationship: Same-chapter Bethabara-Sara-Besana cluster within Benjamin's first city block
rationale: Bethabara, Sara and Besana continue the Benjamin catalog introduced by Jericho and closed with Karapha through Gaba and the supplied twelve-city notice; no alternate names or corrected total are imposed.

relationship: Same-chapter Aiin-Phara-Ephrathah entry before the first block's closure
rationale: Aiin, Phara and Ephrathah occur before the catalog's stated twelve-city closure; this Ephrathah is not independently equated with the explicitly Bethlehem-identified Judah continuation unit.

relationship: Same-chapter twelve-city notice and its preceding named Benjamin entries
rationale: The Karapha, Kephira, Moni and Gaba unit closes the block introduced by Jericho, Betheglio and Amekasis; all actual names and the supplied twelve-city total remain unchanged rather than arithmetically normalized.

relationship: Gibeon and Beeroth in Benjamin's list and the earlier treaty-city notice
rationale: Both lists explicitly name Gibeon and Beeroth; the earlier notice lists the cities approached after the agreement, while Benjamin's catalog additionally names Ramah and preserves its particular allotment role.

relationship: Same-chapter Massema-Miron-Amoke cluster within Benjamin's second block
rationale: Massema, Miron and Amoke continue the block that ends with Jebus or Jerusalem and Gabaothjarim and its supplied thirteen-city notice, without inventing external identities for these three names.

relationship: Same-chapter Phira-to-Thareela entry and second-block conclusion
rationale: Phira, Kaphan, Nakan, Selekan and Thareela immediately precede the Jebus-Jerusalem closing unit and its thirteen-city total, retaining this particular catalog scope and each supplied form.

relationship: Jebus explicitly identified as Jerusalem in allotment and boundary settings
rationale: Both explicitly identify Jebus with Jerusalem; Joshua18 places it in Benjamin's city list, while Joshua15 uses its ridge in Judah's boundary, preserving those distinct tribal descriptions.
